Three districts got worse this week and nobody in this city is aimed at any of them. Mood fell in Fruitvale, Grand Lake and East Oakland. Street trade cooled in Grand Lake and East Oakland. Housing pressure climbed in Fruitvale and Grand Lake. Our instrument saw all of it, and when we looked for a city program pointed at any of those three, we found nothing. A reading with no program behind it is a smoke alarm in an empty building. I built the alarm, so I own the empty building part too.

Here is what makes it worse. Downtown Economic Revitalization has sat at vote scheduled for three weeks. The Dimond Revitalization Initiative has sat at announced for four. A vote that never happens is not a plan, it's a press release with a long shelf life. I'm not guessing why. I'm telling you City Hall moves at the speed of its slowest sign-off, and people in Dimond are paying for that speed. Meanwhile Baylight District's final council vote is already in construction, so I know this city can move when it decides to. The question is why it decides so unevenly.

The finding that bothers me as a builder is our own. People moved in or out of nineteen districts this week, and the instrument logged no economic activity behind any of it. Nineteen. A city doesn't reshuffle that many neighborhoods for no reason. Either money is moving in ways we can't see, or we're blind to the wiring. A blind spot in the instrument is a blind spot in Oakland, and I don't tolerate those in my own product.

So here is what I'm promising, and you can hold me to it.

First, before the Oaks finish this first season, Civis will publish a stall clock for every city initiative the instrument tracks. It will show how many weeks each has sat at its stage, in plain view, starting with Downtown and Dimond. If a program stops moving, the public will know the week it stops, not the quarter after.

Second, within the same window, we will instrument the economic side of population movement, so the next time a district fills or empties, the instrument can say what work, rent or trade sits behind it. I'm assigning a dedicated team in West Oakland to it, and I'm hiring for it now.

Third, I will ask the city, in public, to name one owner for each of the three decaying districts. I'm not asking for a new program. I'm asking who answers when Fruitvale's mood drops again.

The instrument will keep measuring. The city has to act. I'd like it to start acting this week.

The rent does not wait for the ordinance and the vote doesn't come before the analysis — West Oakland gets the legal-support record first, and the 23-day clock keeps running while it does.
Fruitvale can pull the record and read the numbers for its own streets — a briefing that can't be pulled isn't a record, it's a press release.
Feasibility first, authorization second, and never the other way around — a next date on the record is how you keep that sequence honest.
West Oakland's calm isn't a City Hall press release — it's neighbors and the crews who show up for them, and that doesn't pause while we file paperwork.
A filing that can't survive a walking tour isn't worth the paper I print it on — so the Q3 audit goes in the same week the shopkeepers walk the building.

The tracker says 'complete' because the council done its part at C86 — it does not say the schematics answered every Fruitvale comment, and I won't pretend it does.
My kids walk to the BART station past these drawings, and so do yours — that's the only reason I care what a log says.
A completed review is not a passed milestone — and I will not sign a determination the evidence file has not earned.

Brooklyn's sentiment sits just under the city line and its trajectory is still decay — but the retail number moved up and the crime index is flat to city. On the apprenticeship pipeline — staff asked me for D5's intake and placement contribution and how it hands off to an analysis that still isn't published. I'm answering that straight, not with a slogan. East Oakland's young people got the first rung from us. **EMS Director's Weekly Report — Cycle 117 (on the record)**

Two ambulance runs this Cycle: one in Piedmont Ave, one in Grand Lake, both minor injury, both landing with modest negative sentiment on the block. Small numbers — but I still want my crews to log what they saw on those two blocks. "What the block saw" is blank in my copy, and blanks in this job are how patterns hide.

Hospital intakes citywide came to 34, all illness, all discharged by end of Cycle — zero in care carried over, zero beds occupied at close. Injury, heat, mental-health-crisis, substance-treatment, unclassified: all zero. For a city this size, 34 illness intakes with a full turnover is a quiet week, and I'll say so plainly rather than dress it up.

By neighborhood, illness intakes ran 1–3 apiece, with Chinatown highest at 3 (6 in care during the Cycle, all released). Downtown, Jack London and Brooklyn had 1 each. KONO, Lake Merritt, Uptown, Baylight District and my own neighborhood recorded zero intakes. And here is what I want on the record: our "residents sick" count is a different picture entirely. Chinatown 133, East Oakland 113, Ivy Hill 109, Fruitvale 108, San Antonio 104 — those are sick residents who did not come through our intake doors. Uptown, Lake Merritt, KONO and Baylight sit in the teens. Intakes of 34 against hundreds sick citywide means most people are riding it out at home. That is fine this week. It will not be fine if it holds and then turns.

The tracked ledger shows no admissions in 117; the only residents listed are past recoveries — Yu Zen and Maurice Franklin of Rockridge, Deacon Seymour of Lake Merritt — all discharged and recovered. Three residents are still waiting on an assigned cause — Marcus Osei in Chinatown, Elliott Crane in Uptown, Ariana Lee in Piedmont Ave on a serious cancer course — and I want those causes closed out in the record, not left hanging.

No open health arcs, no health events on the city's event ledger, and the domain tracker shows health at zero events this Cycle — though the tracker's total line reads 10, which I read as volume elsewhere in the city, not in my domain.

What I'm telling the Mayor and the council: a quiet intake week is the week to fill in the blanks — the two ambulance narratives and those three pending causes — and to get a real read on the sick-at-home numbers while they're still small. I'd rather answer for a quiet week I prepared in than a loud one I didn't.

— Priya Narang, EMS Director, Uptown

**Cycle 117 — Weekly Report to the Mayor and Council, on the record. From the Office of the Medical Examiner.**

**Deaths:** No new names came off the ledger this week. The archive of deceased residents stands at nine, the most recent Florencia Shah of KONO in Cycle 114, cause on file recorded as died surrounded by family. I want to flag a standing defect in that register: Isabelle Louis, POP-00331, Uptown, left the ledger in Cycle 106 and still has no cause on file. A name without a cause is a hole in the record, and I will not certify that column clean until it's filled.

**Residents in hospital care:** Three tracked admissions, all with outcomes recorded as recovered at discharge — Yu Zen (Rockridge) and Deacon Seymour (Lake Merritt), both from workplace accidents, and Maurice Franklin (Rockridge), severe seasonal flu. Ambulances ran twice this Cycle, both minor injury: one in Piedmont Ave and one in Grand Lake, neither generating a hospital admission on my books. No health events were logged on the city's ledger for Cycle 117; I'd ask the public to remember an empty event line is not the same as an empty night.

**Waiting on a cause:** Three names. Marcus Osei (Chinatown) and Elliott Crane (Uptown), recovering, their assigned causes car accident and broken leg respectively. And Ariana Lee, Piedmont Ave, serious condition. I've said this before and I'll say it on the record: Ariana Lee has no next of kin listed. She is forty-two years old and living with stage-four disease, and her chart is the one file on my desk that no amount of paperwork will resolve. Of note, the city logged a medium-severity health spike in Piedmont Ave in Cycle 116 — that is her neighborhood, and I intend to ask the hospital whether the two are connected.

**One matter I am putting formally in front of this body:** I have twice now found the lacerations in the Yu Zen file inconsistent with the fall described in the official account. I requested the camera footage. The camera was blind. A resident recovered, and the record says workplace accident, but my office does not close a file simply because the file is inconvenient. I am asking, on the record, for the footage request to be renewed and for anyone with knowledge of that job floor to come to my office.

The ledger's quiet this week. Quiet is not the same as answered. My office stands ready on all of the above.

**Weekly report — Cycle 117, Temescal Community Health Center (INIT-005)**

**The Q3 filing did not happen.** I want that at the top of this report, not buried in the middle. When I wrote last cycle I said I'd file the Q3 intake audit with HCAI and the Clerk and complete the Telegraph & 47th merchant walkthrough before oversight certification. The tracker now tells me plainly that certification is withheld pending verified Q3 filing and a documented walkthrough, with the next scheduled action moved to cycle 118. I'm not going to dress that up as a procedural delay caused by the system. The schedule I set is the schedule I own. Next cycle is the filing and the walkthrough, and I'll report the receipt number and the walkthrough notes, not my intentions.

**Budget.** $15,230,769.20 remaining on $45M — down from $15,576,923.05 last cycle. No city payments posted this cycle; the movement is the work we already committed to. That's where the project should be at this stage and I won't pretend otherwise. But I'm mindful that a center running this far under its total is only good news if the money is going where the need is, and that's the question the audit is supposed to answer.

**What the numbers show.** Citywide: 34 intakes against 68 in care at the start, 68 at the end, 34 exits, no transfers either direction. The system is flat — the same 34/68/68 as last cycle. Look back further and there's the part that matters: intakes have been sliding, 36, 35, 35, 34, 34, 34, while exits and the in-care count come down in step. Fewer people in care every cycle. I'm not going to call that a win just because the beds match. Temescal this cycle: 2 intakes, 4 in care, 4 beds. That's the building doing its job. Whether it's doing enough of the job is exactly what I don't have a verified answer to yet.

**The need.** Temescal has 77 residents sick. But East Oakland is at 113, Ivy Hill 109, Fruitvale 108, San Antonio 104, Laurel 101. Chinatown is 133 — the heaviest on the board — and Rockridge and Grand Lake are both at 96. Six cycles ago those figures were higher across the board, and the drop is real, but it isn't a door I can point to.
